notes: Corrected, from-scratch redraft addressing two fact-check omissions: (1) Micah 7:18-20, the closing "who is a God like unto thee" pardon hymn, now has its own law tier (divine_mercy_pardon) rather than being absent; (2) Micah 6:16 (Omri and "the house of Ahab" named as the source of Judah's wicked statutes) is now cited within the covenant_lawsuit tier's verses. The five submanagers (Moses, Aaron, Miriam, Balak, Balaam) are cited exactly as Micah 6:4-5 states them, with no invented narrative detail imported from Exodus/Numbers beyond what Micah's own text supplies. Naming collision flagged: this Micah (1:1) is not the Micah of Judges 17-18, despite identical KJV spelling. No KJV spelling variants (e.g. Omri/Ahab, Balak/Balaam) needed flagging in this book — all names here match their spelling in every other KJV occurrence.

characters.name: Micah
characters.perkNote: The prophet whose scroll opens and closes the book — owning this tier is the prerequisite for every oracle tier below.

genealogy.note: No father, mother, spouse, or children are named for Micah in scripture; 'the Morasthite' (Micah 1:1) identifies his hometown of Moresheth (cf. 1:14), not a family line.

verses.note: Superscription: the word of the LORD that came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.
Micah's own dramatic response to the coming judgment: 'Therefore I will wail and howl, I will go stripped and naked: I will make a wailing like the dragons, and mourning as the owls.'
Micah's declaration of his own prophetic authority: 'I am full of power by the spirit of the LORD, and of judgment, and of might, to declare unto Jacob his transgression, and to Israel his sin.'
Micah's personal statement of hope preceding the closing hymn: 'Therefore I will look unto the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me.'

funFacts: Micah prophesied in Judah during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (Micah 1:1), making him a contemporary of Isaiah.

Jeremiah 26:18 quotes Micah 3:12 by name over a century later, crediting 'Micah the Morasthite' — one of the few Old Testament instances of one prophet's exact words being cited and attributed to him by another book.

NAMING COLLISION: this Micah is not the same person as the Micah of Judges 17-18 (the Ephraimite who made a household idol) — identical KJV spelling, unrelated individual, roughly four centuries apart.

characters.name: Judgment Against Corrupt Leaders
characters.purpose: Indicts Judah's civic and religious leadership — rulers who abhor justice, prophets who divine for money yet claim the LORD's protection, priests who teach for hire — declaring that because of their corruption Zion will be plowed as a field and Jerusalem will become heaps.
characters.perkNote: Highlights the book's indictment of bribed rulers, hired priests, and prophets who divine for money.

verses.note: Condemns Israel's 'heads of Jacob, and princes of the house of Israel' who 'hate the good, and love the evil,' described figuratively as devouring their own people's flesh.
Condemns prophets 'that make my people err, that bite with their teeth, and cry, Peace; and he that putteth not into their mouths, they even prepare war against him.'

'The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon the LORD, and say, Is not the LORD among us? none evil can come upon us.'

'Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest' — quoted by name a century later in Jeremiah 26:18.

funFacts: Micah 3:12 is quoted by name in Jeremiah 26:18, where elders recall 'Micah the Morasthite' prophesying under Hezekiah that 'Zion shall be plowed like a field,' citing it as precedent that a doom-prophet need not be put to death for the words alone.

The oracle's language of leaders who 'pluck off their skin from off them, and their flesh from off their bones' (3:2-3) is figurative indictment of exploitation, not a description of any literal act carried out in the passage.

characters.name: The Mountain of the LORD's House
characters.purpose: Envisions a future day when the LORD's house is exalted above all mountains and nations stream to it to learn His ways, converting weapons of war into farming tools and living in secure peace — a promise of universal peace under God's law, worded almost identically to Isaiah's temple-mountain oracle.
characters.perkNote: Represents the swords-into-plowshares vision of nations at peace under God's law.

verses.note: 'In the last days... the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established in the top of the mountains... for the law shall go forth of Zion, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.'
'They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up a sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.'
'But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid' — a vision of secure, individual peace under the coming reign of God's law.

funFacts: Micah 4:1-3 is worded almost identically to Isaiah 2:2-4 — one of the closest word-for-word parallels between two different prophetic books in the Old Testament; scripture does not state which prophet spoke it first.
'Every man under his vine and under his fig tree' (4:4) became a standalone idiom for peaceful prosperity, echoed again in 1 Kings 4:25 (of Solomon's reign) and Zechariah 3:10.

characters.name: Bethlehem's Promised Ruler
characters.purpose: Names Bethlehem Ephratah, though little among Judah's clans, as the origin of a future ruler in Israel whose goings forth are 'from of old, from everlasting'; promises this ruler will stand and feed his flock in the strength of the LORD, becoming Israel's peace.
characters.perkNote: Represents the promised ruler from Bethlehem Ephratah, 'whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.'

verses.note: 'But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.'
'And he shall stand and feed in the strength of the LORD... and they shall abide: for now shall he be great unto the ends of the earth.'
'And this man shall be the peace' — names the coming ruler's role explicitly as Israel's peace.

funFacts: Quoted directly by name in Matthew 2:6, where Jerusalem's chief priests and scribes cite Micah 5:2 to identify Bethlehem as the Messiah's birthplace in answer to Herod's question.
Micah 5:2 calls the town 'Bethlehem Ephratah' — the fuller, older form of the name (cf. Genesis 35:19, Ruth 1:2) distinguishing it from a second, unrelated Bethlehem in Zebulun (Joshua 19:15).

characters.name: The LORD's Covenant Lawsuit
characters.deliveredBy: Micah, voicing the LORD's covenant controversy (rib) against His people
characters.purpose: A formal covenant lawsuit in which the LORD summons the mountains and hills as witnesses, recounts His redemptive acts (bringing Israel up from Egypt, sending Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, overturning Balak's plot with Balaam) as evidence of His own righteousness, rejects empty ritual sacrifice as a substitute for obedience, and defines true covenant faithfulness as doing justly, loving mercy, and walking humbly with God — followed by a sentence pronounced (6:9-16) against the city's violence, deceitful commerce, and its adherence to 'the statutes of Omri, and all the works of the house of Ahab.'
characters.perkNote: Represents the LORD's formal covenant lawsuit, summoning mountains and hills as witnesses against Israel's breach.

verses.note: The LORD's rib (lawsuit) opens: 'Arise, contend thou before the mountains... Hear ye, O mountains, the LORD's controversy, and ye strong foundations of the earth: for the LORD hath a controversy with his people.'

God's evidence for His own righteousness: 'I brought thee up out of the land of Egypt... and I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. O my people, remember now what Balak king of Moab consulted, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him from Shittim unto Gilgal; that ye may know the righteousness of the LORD.'
Rhetorical rejection of empty ritual: 'Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression...?'
The book's most quoted verse: 'He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?'
'Shall I count them pure with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights?' — indicting fraudulent commerce as part of the sentence.

The sentence closes by naming the source of Judah's corruption: 'For the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab, and ye walk in their counsels' — indicting the nation for institutionalizing the wicked precedent of King Omri and the house of Ahab (cf. 1 Kings 16), resulting in desolation, hissing, and reproach.

funFacts: Micah 6:8 is one of the most frequently quoted single verses from any Minor Prophet — 'to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God' — summarizing covenant obedience without naming a single ritual requirement.

The 'rib' (controversy/lawsuit) form Micah uses in 6:1-5, summoning mountains and hills as legal witnesses, mirrors the same covenant-lawsuit pattern found in Deuteronomy 32:1 and Isaiah 1:2, where heaven and earth are called to witness Israel's breach of covenant.

characters.name: Who Is A God Like Unto Thee
characters.purpose: The book's closing hymn of praise, asking 'who is a God like unto thee' who pardons iniquity and delights in mercy rather than retaining anger forever, and promising that God will subdue Israel's iniquities and cast all their sins into the depths of the sea, fulfilling the truth sworn to Jacob and the mercy sworn to Abraham from days of old.
characters.perkNote: Represents the closing hymn of pardon — 'thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.'

verses.note: 'Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy.'
'He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.'

'Thou wilt perform the truth to Jacob, and the mercy to Abraham, which thou hast sworn unto our fathers from the days of old' — closing the book by grounding God's mercy in the patriarchal covenant oaths to Jacob and Abraham.

funFacts: Micah 7:18 plays on the prophet's own name — 'Micah' (Mikayahu) means 'Who is like the LORD?' — and the verse opens 'Who is a God like unto thee' (Mi-El-kamokha), tying the book's closing hymn back to the prophet's own identity.

This closing hymn (7:18-20) is associated in later Jewish practice with Tashlich, a Rosh Hashanah observance where verse 19's 'cast all their sins into the depths of the sea' is recited near a body of water — a matter of reception history, not part of Micah's own text.

characters.name: Moses
characters.perkNote: Cited as one of the three leaders God sent to redeem Israel from Egypt, offered as evidence of the LORD's righteousness in His covenant lawsuit (6:4).

genealogy.note: Micah names Moses only as one of three leaders sent by God (6:4); his parentage (Amram and Jochebed, Exodus 6:20) and full family line are established elsewhere, outside Micah's own text.

verses.note: 'I brought thee up out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed thee out of the house of servants; and I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.'

funFacts: Named directly in Micah 6:4 as one of the three leaders 'sent before' Israel out of Egypt, cited as evidence in the LORD's covenant lawsuit rather than given any new narrative detail.

characters.name: Aaron
characters.perkNote: Cited alongside Moses and Miriam as one of the leaders God sent before Israel, part of the evidence of God's righteousness (6:4).

genealogy.note: Micah names Aaron only alongside Moses and Miriam as one sent by God (6:4); his priestly lineage is established in Exodus, outside Micah's own text.

verses.note: Named as the second of the three leaders God 'sent before' Israel: 'I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.'

funFacts: Named alongside Moses and Miriam in Micah 6:4; Micah adds no priestly or narrative detail beyond the bare name, unlike his extensive role in Exodus and Leviticus.

characters.name: Miriam
characters.perkNote: Cited as the third of the leaders God sent before Israel, part of the evidence of God's righteousness in the covenant lawsuit (6:4).

genealogy.note: Micah names Miriam as the third leader sent by God (6:4); her fuller story is told in Exodus and Numbers, outside Micah's own text.

verses.note: Named as the third of the three leaders God 'sent before' Israel: 'I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.'

funFacts: The only woman named in the book of Micah, listed as one of Israel's three sent leaders in Micah 6:4 — a direct scriptural affirmation of her leadership alongside her brothers (cf. Exodus 15:20, Numbers 12).

characters.name: Balak
characters.perkNote: Cited as the Moabite king whose plot to curse Israel through Balaam is recalled as evidence that the LORD preserved Israel's righteousness (6:5).

genealogy.note: Identified only by title, 'Balak king of Moab' (Micah 6:5); no genealogy is given in Micah itself (cf. Numbers 22:2-4 for his introduction).

verses.note: 'O my people, remember now what Balak king of Moab consulted, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him from Shittim unto Gilgal; that ye may know the righteousness of the LORD.'

funFacts: King of Moab who hired Balaam to curse Israel (full account in Numbers 22-24); Micah 6:5 recalls the episode only in summary, as proof that the LORD preserved Israel despite the plot.
'Balak' appears only this once in Micah, spelled identically to every other KJV occurrence (Numbers, Joshua, Judges, Revelation) — no spelling variant to flag.

characters.name: Balaam
characters.perkNote: Cited alongside Balak as the hired prophet consulted at Shittim, recalled to demonstrate 'the righteousness of the LORD' (6:5).

genealogy.note: Micah itself names his father — 'Balaam the son of Beor' (6:5) — the only patronymic given for any figure in this book besides Micah's own gentilic. No further genealogy is stated here.

verses.note: 'What Balaam the son of Beor answered him from Shittim unto Gilgal; that ye may know the righteousness of the LORD.'

funFacts: NAMING COLLISION / CONTINUITY: same Balaam son of Beor as in Numbers 22-24, Deuteronomy 23:4-5, Joshua 24:9-10, Judges 11:25, Nehemiah 13:2, and cited again in the New Testament (2 Peter 2:15, Jude 1:11, Revelation 2:14) as a byword for a prophet who loved a wicked reward — Micah's own citation is notably neutral and evidentiary, naming him only to demonstrate 'the righteousness of the LORD' (6:5), not to condemn him.
Micah 6:5 is the only verse in the book that supplies a place name for the episode, 'from Shittim unto Gilgal' — marking the stretch of Israel's journey the remembrance covers.
